prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 classification of time-reversal-invariant insulators, and for the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state, establishing band topology as an organizing principle of electronic matter.

statement.case_for: After the full exchange I keep the Kane, Mele and Molenkamp configuration. The scientific core has not been challenged by anyone: the Z2 invariant and protected helical edge states form a robust, disorder-surviving statement about band structure, which is what I as a statistical physicist find most convincing, and it was confirmed by a decisive transport experiment and then by fifteen to twenty years of independent work in many materials with transport and spectroscopic probes. Interpretation is stable, in contrast with magic-angle graphene. The chair's question about whether the citation can stand on its own has a workable answer: word it around the quantum spin Hall prediction, the Z2 classification and the first observation, and explicitly not around the HgTe proposal, three-dimensional topological insulators or the quantum anomalous Hall effect. The 2016 prize honoured topological phase transitions and quantised Hall conductance in systems that break time-reversal symmetry or are one-dimensional or two-dimensional models; the time-reversal-invariant insulator with protected boundary modes is a different physical statement, so I do not regard this as a repeat. On the chair's central question, I decide for breadth of conceptual influence combined with a stable interpretation, provided the attribution gap is stated openly rather than hidden.
statement.case_against: I take the attribution objection more seriously than in round 1. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal is what told Molenkamp which material and which thickness to use, and with Zhang deceased the omission cannot be repaired. A citation can avoid claiming the HgTe proposal, but it cannot give it credit, and a sceptic can say that the prize rewards the experiment that confirmed a prediction by people it does not name. The 3D strand (Fu, Kane, Mele; Hasan) and the quantum anomalous Hall effect (Xue) are also left out, and the 2016 prize still lies close enough that some members will read this as a second topology prize. Applications remain mostly prospective. Against this, B022 has the cleaner credit tree, and if the committee concludes that an incomplete attribution is disqualifying, then lattice clocks are the stronger fallback and I would vote for them before the graphene ballot.

responses.point: Pearce argues that a prize which has to leave out two or three people with a strong claim (Mele, Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) is a weaker construct than a two-person prize with a clean division of credit, and notes that my round-1 trio omitted Mele only in my opening ballot.
responses.response: Mele is in my trio now, so that part is settled, and I agree that attribution clarity is a real criterion. But I do not think the comparison is as lopsided as you put it. B022 also leaves out Lemonde, Takamoto, Hollberg, Derevianko and the Yb and Hg groups, and you yourself note the contest between Katori and Ye over the 10^-18 regime. Both ballots have a credit tail; the difference is that in B045 the missing names belong to one proposal that guided one experiment, while the core division, Kane and Mele for the theory and Molenkamp for the observation, is unambiguous. I give clarity of attribution weight, but not enough to outweigh a difference in kind: topological band theory changed how a whole field classifies and searches for matter, whereas the lattice clock is an outstanding improvement of an instrument inside a line already prized in 2005 and 2012. That is why I keep B045 first while ranking your ballot as my first alternative.

responses.point: Kroll holds optical lattice clocks first as an instrument-level advance with stable interpretation and now discloses the Hall-laboratory stay, saying the committee may need to consider recusal; he and Pearce regard the unredefined SI second as not a precondition.
responses.response: I asked in round 1 whether the redefinition is a precondition, and I accept your answer that it is not: the clocks have already delivered tests of constants and geodesy, so the case does not depend on a metrological decision outside physics. That removes one of my own doubts about timing and I record it as a point in favour of B022. I also think your disclosure is handled correctly as a disclosed bias, since you report no collaboration with Katori or Ye and the Hall connection is a lineage link; I would not ask for formal recusal, and I would only note that the four-member B022 bloc includes the member with the most direct field proximity. My remaining disagreement is the criterion: an instrument record, however spectacular, is not for me the same kind of discovery as a new protected state of matter, and an accuracy that the next generation of clocks will probably surpass is a less stable object of recognition than an invariant.

responses.point: Olsson treats the lattice-clock case as the cleanest datable invention with a two-person credit and counts the incomplete B045 credit tree as a fairness cost, noting that the 2005 and 2012 prizes make a clock prize look like a third award in one lineage.
responses.response: I agree with you that B022 is a datable invention with a clear credit, and that its downstream uses are realised rather than promised, which is more than I can say for topological applications. But your own against-case concedes that a third metrology award is a risk, and I weigh that risk more than you do. On the fairness cost of B045, I think wording the citation around the quantum spin Hall prediction and observation limits the harm: it names what Kane, Mele and Molenkamp did and does not claim what Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang did. I also do not accept that fairness is cleanly better served by B022, because the Katori and Ye credit split and the unnamed Lemonde and Takamoto groups raise the same question. I therefore still see this as a real difference of weighting between us and not as an argument that settles it.

responses.point: Danielsson holds twisted bilayer graphene first as a rare theory-then-experiment case and now says the flat-band origin is stable even though the pairing mechanism is not, accepting that Cao, Fatemi and others are outside the credited names.
responses.response: I agree that the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 experiment is an unusually clean sequence, and that the platform is highly productive. My difficulty remains what the committee would be recognising: the stable part, the flat bands at the magic angle, is the prediction, while the experimental discoveries that give the prize its weight, correlated insulators and superconductivity, are exactly the part whose origin and dependence on disorder are not settled. In addition, Cao and Fatemi, the first authors who carried out the experiment, cannot be named under a three-person limit with Bistritzer included. I would be prepared to see B030 in a prize in perhaps five to ten years, when the mechanism question has narrowed, and keep it as my second alternative, and I do not consider the objection a judgment on its merit.

responses.point: Johansson moved to the Kane, Mele and Molenkamp trio and names B022 as the clean two-person fallback that he would not stand in the way of; he also treats the 2016 prize as covering distinct work.
responses.response: I agree with your reading of the 2016 prize and I want to hold you to the fallback: I would likewise not oppose B022 if the committee decides that the unrepaired attribution gap in B045 is disqualifying. Where I differ slightly is on how openly that should be said. I think the citation and the committee statement should explicitly mention the HgTe proposal as context and say that the prize concerns the quantum spin Hall effect, instead of relying on silence. If members prefer wording that appears to cover the whole topological-insulator field, I would raise my attribution concern, because that is where the claim would exceed what three names can carry.

uncertainties: How a three-person limit can fairly acknowledge the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal when Zhang is deceased and the others are outside the credited names; wording can avoid overclaiming but cannot give credit.

Whether the committee would treat the 2016 prize as close enough to make a second topology prize premature; I judge the physics distinct but this is a matter of weighting that colleagues reasonably dispute.

Whether breadth of conceptual influence should outweigh a cleaner two-person attribution in B022; this is the central difference between the B045 and B022 groups and I do not think either side can show it is wrong.
How the committee should treat the disclosed Hall-laboratory link of Kroll on B022 and the Chalmers links of Johansson and Olsson on B039, and whether disclosure suffices.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict or recusal is apparent from my profile. I have no documented personal or institutional tie to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan, Katori, Ye or the other shortlisted candidates, and my own research areas in statistical physics, random matrices, turbulence and neural networks are not subjects of any shortlisted ballot. I note the disclosures of other members in round 1 and have no objection to treating them as disclosed bias instead of recusal, apart from Johansson's stated recusal on B039, which I support.
